title: 5 Smart Ways to Handle Office Politics (Without the Drama)
author: Gaurav Jain
summary: Jain argues that office politics is not optional and that good managers who try to stay out of it end up sidelined. He offers five trap-and-fix pairs: fairness is not sameness, avoid conflict avoidance, map invisible power structures, share strategically rather than reactively, and do not assume results speak for themselves. Each fix leans on a named framework such as Situational Leadership, Radical Candor, the Power-Influence Matrix, or the STAR technique. His thesis is that the problem is unawareness, not politics itself, and that smart intentional engagement does not require manipulation. He closes by asking whether the reader is avoiding politics or avoiding leadership.
points: Treating everyone identically can feel careless to a team; fairness means equity, so leaders should flex their style to each person's development level.
Conflict avoidance buys short-term harmony but seeds long-term dysfunction and leaves the manager looking like someone who does not protect the team.
Informal power, the shadow org chart of who people go to for advice and alignment, shapes decisions, so leaders must build authentic relationships with those nodes.
Transparency without discretion becomes a liability in political environments; Jain proposes testing audience, timing, context and misinterpretation risk before sharing.
Perception shapes opportunity as much as performance, so leaders need to own their narrative by sharing team wins.
quotes: Office politics isn’t optional. Whether you play or not, the game is being played around you.
The Trap: Avoiding conflict might buy you short-term harmony, but it seeds long-term dysfunction. You become the manager who doesn’t protect their team.
The Trap: Treating everyone the same can come across as tone-deaf, especially when people need different levels of support. In high-pressure environments, sameness ≠ fairness.
These are the nodes of what I call the shadow org chart, and you need to build authentic relationships with them.
The Trap: Thinking your work will automatically earn recognition. In reality, perception shapes opportunity more than performance alone.
Most political traps aren’t created by malicious intent. They’re created by good managers trying to lead on principles, without realizing the hidden dynamics around them.
